name: ASPCA: farm animals
beneficiaries_note: Our build: US hens and sows.
summary: The ASPCA's farm animal welfare team, a small part of its $422m spending in 2025 (about $8m with its share of public education, our judgment), lobbied against federal and state rollbacks of the laws that keep hens out of cages and sows out of crates, and pushed shoppers, farmers and producers toward higher-welfare products and in-ovo sexed eggs. At the site's defaults it comes to about 0.00004 years of healthy life per $1,000, far below the median animal charity because the defence, which matters for some 70 million hens, is shared with a coalition in which the ASPCA's own spending (about $1.5m of lobbying and outreach) is a small part, its 2025 work moved the chance of an override only a little, and its large reserves make the next dollar worth less than the average. The biggest uncertainties are those chances and the share of the ASPCA's policy spending that goes on farm animals, which the accounts don't give; the result is mostly uncertainty, spanning several orders of magnitude, and both branches are discounted for missing outcome data.

sections.title: In chicken pain days
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for every animal model. The shared SAD figures are Ambitious Impact's, which count each species' pain as a share of a person's with its own species weights. Here those weights come out and Rethink Priorities' go in, so every species is counted in days of a chicken's disabling pain. How a chicken compares with a person is the one animal slider.

The ASPCA's lobbying on every issue, 2025

source.title: ASPCA Form 990 for 2025
source.page: Schedule C, Part II-B, line 1j (total of lines 1a-1i)

rows.explainer: Media $81,594, mailings $39,805, publications $7,772, grants for lobbying $216,967, direct contact $784,388, rallies and lobby days $122,772, other $597,316: every issue, from puppy mills, horse slaughter, housing and telehealth to the farm laws.

rows.label: Share of the ASPCA's 2025 lobbying spent defending farm-animal laws
rows.explainer: Our judgment: Schedule O names, for 2025, three California puppy-mill laws, New York's pet-shop law, the SAFE Act on horse slaughter, housing, telehealth and disaster bills beside the farm preemption fight, the largest single federal campaign. 40%, 25% to 60%.

rows.label: Defence work not reported as lobbying, 2025
rows.explainer: Our judgment: the farm team's coalition work, farmer outreach (the farmers it gathered on Proposition 12 before the July 2025 House hearing) and communications on the defence that fall outside the lobbying definition; a few staff's time at about $150,000 each with overheads, the anchor of facts/aspca.json. $0.8m, $0.3m to $2m. The rest of the farm budget is the market branch, the Crate Free Illinois grant and the opposition to faster slaughter lines; the last two won nothing in 2025 and add no modelled outcome.

rows.label: State repeal fights won, as a multiple of the federal defence
rows.explainer: Our judgment from the ASPCA's review of the year: repeal bills in Colorado and Michigan (whose laws cover over 12 million birds) 'failed to gain any traction', so they were at small risk; Arizona's governor vetoed a repeal but the law was already delayed to 2034, outside the years counted; Nevada passed an emergency suspension. 1.02, 1 to 1.1.

Share of the animals under the laws that would go back into cages or crates within the years counted if the laws fell
rows.explainer: Our judgment, as in charityevals' models of The Humane League (the same fight): in-state housing laws and company pledges would keep most cage-free and crate-free supply, and barns already built rarely go back to cages; replacement barns, buyers without pledges and price pressure after bird flu would bring some back.

rows.label: Chance a federal override of the state laws passes without the coalition's 2025 opposition
rows.explainer: Our judgment, as in charityevals' models of The Humane League: EATS-style language was in the House Farm Bill drafts of 2024-25, and ahead of the July 2025 House Agriculture hearing on Proposition 12 the ASPCA gathered farmers' testimony against it; the coalition (Humane World for Animals, the ASPCA, The Humane League and others) gathered letters from more than 200 members of Congress against it. Without that opposition we put an override in the next Farm Bill at 30%. One event, drawn as happens or doesn't.

source.title: ASPCA press release: U.S. House Agriculture Committee holds hearing on Proposition 12 (July 2025)
source.quote: calling on Congress to protect state animal protection laws that have improved the lives of millions of farm animals

rows.label: Chance it passes with the coalition's 2025 opposition
rows.explainer: Our judgment, as in charityevals' models of The Humane League (the same event): the year's opposition takes about 5 points off (a sixth of the risk). Research on lobbying finds most campaigns change nothing (Baumgartner and colleagues, 2009); organised constituent contact moved legislators' support by about 12 points in a field experiment (Bergan and Cole, 2015). Drawn together with the chance without it.

Market: hen-years a year in the shift the ASPCA's guide, farmer work and in-ovo advocacy touch (before what would have happened anyway and others' share)
rows.explainer: Our judgment. The ASPCA's Shop With Your Heart guide steers shoppers and buyers to eggs, chicken, pork and beef under meaningful welfare certifications, it works with independent higher-welfare farmers, its Fund to End Factory Farming gave $160,305 to seven projects in 2025 (community and environmental groups opposing factory-farm pollution), and it championed in-ovo sexed eggs, on sale in 15 states from 2025 (Form 990 Schedule O, line 4c). It publishes no count of animals affected. We express it as hens moved from cages to cage-free housing: 300,000 hen-years a year (about 0.1% of the flock), 50,000 to 2 million.

rows.explainer: Our judgment: in-ovo sexing spares male chicks being hatched and killed on the first day. Deaths are not suffering on the site's scale, so only the hatchery handling and killing, minutes for each chick, count; with the sexed eggs still a small share of sales, a few percent of the branch, 0 to 15%.
